subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia in adolescent girl
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 15 year old girl brought by her mother for tiredness that has worsened over three months. She is falling asleep in afternoon classes and has stopped athletics training. Her periods began at 12 and for the last year have lasted seven days with heavy flow requiring a pad every two hours on the first two days. She eats a self-described vegetarian diet with no red meat and drinks two mugs of tea with lunch.

She reports no bruising, no black stools, no weight loss, no recurrent infections. She is not sexually active. There is no family history of thalassaemia or coeliac disease.

On examination she has pale conjunctivae and mild angular cheilitis; the remainder of the examination including abdominal palpation is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (120-160), MCV 71 fL (80-100), MCH 22 pg (27-32), platelets 384 x10^9/L (150-400), white cells 6.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), ferritin 6 microg/L (30-200), transferrin saturation 8% (20-45), CRP <5 mg/L (<5), coeliac serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence oral ferrous sulfate 100 mg elemental iron on alternate days with vitamin C and arrange menstrual review
options.rationale: Alternate-day oral iron in confirmed iron deficiency (ferritin 6, transferrin saturation 8%) improves fractional absorpt. (Source: eTG: Iron deficiency; RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Commence oral ferrous sulfate 100 mg elemental iron daily and repeat full blood count in six weeks
options.rationale: Daily dosing produces a hepcidin rise that halves fractional absorption of the next dose, so alternate-day dosing gives. (Source: eTG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Arrange an intravenous iron carboxymaltose infusion in the day-oncology unit within the week
options.rationale: IV iron in adolescents is reserved for oral intolerance, malabsorption, ongoing loss exceeding oral replacement, or need. (Source: AMH: Iron replacement)

options.text: Refer for upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy before starting iron replacement
options.rationale: Endoscopy is indicated in adolescents with iron deficiency when there is no identifiable cause and menstrual and dietary. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Trial ferrous sulfate 100 mg twice daily with meals and add proton pump inhibitor for gastric protection
options.rationale: Twice-daily dosing worsens hepcidin-driven absorption blockade, meals reduce iron uptake, and proton pump inhibitors red. (Source: eTG: Iron deficiency)

explanation.summary: Adolescent iron deficiency anaemia is common in menstruating girls and is compounded by vegetarian diet and tannin-rich beverages that block non-haem iron absorption.
key_points: Alternate-day oral iron beats daily dosing for absorption and tolerability in non-pregnant women and.
Vitamin C co-administration doubles fractional iron absorption; tea, milk, calcium and PPIs reduce i.
IV iron reserved for oral intolerance, malabsorption, or losses exceeding oral replacement capacity.
explanation.pearls: Ferrous sulfate 100 mg elemental iron on alternate days achieves better 14-day cumulative absorption than 100 mg daily because hepcidin blocks absorption for ar.

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis escalation of respiratory support
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a metropolitan emergency department reviewing a 6 month old boy brought in by ambulance with three days of coryza, cough and worsening breathing since this morning. He is bottle-fed and today has taken only half his usual volumes with brief episodes where he pulls off and pants. He has had no fever, no apnoeas witnessed, and no wheeze audible to the parents. He was born at 38 weeks by uncomplicated caesarean and has no comorbidities.

On examination he is alert but working hard: subcostal and intercostal recession, tracheal tug, bilateral fine crackles and expiratory wheeze. Capillary refill is under two seconds and he is well perfused.

He has been on low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min for two hours since triage.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168 /min, respiratory rate 62 /min, SpO2 89% on 1 L/min nasal prong oxygen, temperature 37.4 degC
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal PCR positive for respiratory syncytial virus; venous blood gas pH 7.34 pCO2 48 mmHg (35-45) HCO3 24 mmol/L (22-26) lactate 1.6 mmol/L (<2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in respiratory support?

options.text: Increase nasal prong oxygen to 2 L/min and reassess in one hour with a repeat blood gas
options.rationale: Low-flow nasal prongs deliver an unreliable FiO2 above 2 L/min and there is a ceiling effect around 2 L/min in infants. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Start high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min with FiO2 titrated to SpO2 92 to 96%
options.rationale: Australian bronchiolitis guidance moves to high-flow at 2 L/kg/min when a child has failed a two-hour low-flow trial wit. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg and reassess response before escalating support
options.rationale: Salbutamol is not recommended for bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months because there is no consistent evidence of be. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Administer nebulised 3% hypertonic saline and continue low-flow oxygen for six hours
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is not recommended in Australian bronchiolitis pathways for emergency department infants because the p. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Proceed directly to CPAP at 6 cmH2O in the emergency department resuscitation bay
options.rationale: CPAP is reserved for infants who fail high-flow nasal cannula, or who have impending respiratory failure with hypercapni. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Australian bronchiolitis pathways use a stepped escalation model: room air where possible, then low-flow nasal prong oxygen 1-2 L/min targeting SpO2 90% and above, then high-flow n.
key_points: SpO2 target for bronchiolitis is 90% and above (not 92-94% as in some older guidelines).
Low-flow ceiling is 2 L/min in infants; escalate to HFNC 2 L/kg/min after a 2-hour trial fails.
Salbutamol and hypertonic saline are not routine in Australian bronchiolitis care.
explanation.pearls: In Australian ED bronchiolitis care, escalate to high-flow nasal cannula 2 L/kg/min after 2 hours of failed low-flow (SpO2 <90% or worsening work of breathing).

subtopic_detail: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia phototherapy decision
stem:
You are the neonatal registrar reviewing a term baby girl on the postnatal ward at 54 hours of age. She was born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery weighing 3.6 kg, is exclusively breastfeeding with good latch, and has passed meconium and urine. Her mother is blood group O positive with negative antibody screen; the baby's cord blood group is B positive with a positive direct antiglobulin test. There are no dysmorphic features and no cephalhaematoma.

The midwife has escalated because the baby looks visibly yellow to the face and chest today. A transcutaneous bilirubin reading was 305 micromol/L, prompting a serum sample.

Serum total bilirubin is 320 micromol/L with conjugated fraction 8 micromol/L. Weight loss from birth is 7.4%.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 /min, respiratory rate 42 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert baby, moderate jaundice to chest and abdomen, tone and reflexes normal, no cephalhaematoma, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Serum bilirubin total 320 micromol/L (conjugated 8), haemoglobin 168 g/L (140-220 neonate), reticulocytes 4.5%, ABO incompatibility with positive direct antiglobulin test

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the mother and repeat serum bilirubin in 24 hours because ABO incompatibility is usually mild
options.rationale: Positive DAT with ABO incompatibility lowers the phototherapy threshold on Australasian nomograms because ongoing haemol. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Arrange urgent exchange transfusion via the umbilical vein without further phototherapy
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion is indicated when bilirubin approaches the exchange line despite intensive phototherapy, or where t. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Commence intensive phototherapy now and repeat serum bilirubin in four to six hours
options.rationale: At 54 hours of age, 320 micromol/L in the presence of a haemolysis risk factor (positive DAT with ABO incompatibility) e. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice; ANZCOR)

options.text: Stop breastfeeding for 24 hours and give formula while continuing observation without phototherapy
options.rationale: Interrupting breastfeeding is not the primary intervention here and does not address haemolysis. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Give a single dose of intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg and monitor without phototherapy
options.rationale: IVIG is an adjunct in haemolytic disease of the newborn (isoimmune) with rising bilirubin despite intensive phototherapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Neonatal jaundice management in Australia uses gestational-age and postnatal-age nomograms with lower thresholds when haemolysis risk factors are present (positive DAT, isoimmunisa.
key_points: Positive DAT with ABO incompatibility lowers the phototherapy and exchange thresholds.
Intensive phototherapy is first-line above the phototherapy line, with recheck at 4-6 hours.
Exchange transfusion for continued rise despite phototherapy or acute bilirubin encephalopathy.
explanation.pearls: In ABO incompatibility with positive DAT at 54 hours, intensive phototherapy is triggered around 30 micromol/L below the standard nomogram line; recheck bilirub.

subtopic_detail: Incomplete Kawasaki disease with unilateral cervical adenitis pretender
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a tertiary emergency department reviewing a 4 year old boy referred by his GP with fever for six days and a swollen left neck. He has been treated with oral cefalexin for 48 hours for presumed bacterial cervical lymphadenitis without improvement.

On today's review he is irritable but consolable. He has a 3 cm firm, non-fluctuant left anterior cervical lymph node that is tender but not erythematous. There is bilateral bulbar conjunctival injection without exudate, cracked lips, and a fine erythematous rash on the trunk that his father says began this morning. Hands and feet appear normal.

Urinalysis shows sterile pyuria. Blood cultures at 24 hours are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148 /min, blood pressure 94/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 39.2 degC
data_table.Examination: 3 cm firm left anterior cervical node, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, cracked lips, truncal maculopapular rash, hands and feet normal, no oral ulcers
data_table.Investigations: CRP 132 mg/L (<5), ESR 78 mm/h (<15), platelets 468 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 62 U/L (<40), albumin 30 g/L (35-50), sodium 133 mmol/L (135-145), sterile pyuria, blood cultures negative at 24 h, neck ultrasound: enlarged left cervical node without abscess or discrete collection

lead_in: What is the single best next step in management?

options.text: Continue oral cefalexin and add oral clindamycin to broaden gram-positive cover for atypical adenitis
options.rationale: The clinical picture is inconsistent with staphylococcal or streptococcal cervical lymphadenitis: no fluctuance, no absc. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin and repeat neck ultrasound at 24 hours before other diagnoses
options.rationale: Persisting with bacterial adenitis pathway ignores the incomplete Kawasaki disease pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Give a single dose of intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg and reassess again in 24 hours
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are added upfront only in high-risk Kawasaki disease (Kobayashi or Egami scores predicting IVIG resistan. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Arrange transthoracic echocardiogram and, regardless of coronary findings, commence IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin
options.rationale: This is incomplete Kawasaki disease: fever for at least 5 days with two of five principal criteria (conjunctivitis, oral. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease; AHA scientific statement)
source_refs: AHA scientific statement on Kawasaki disease

options.text: Perform excisional biopsy of the cervical lymph node to exclude atypical mycobacterial infection here
options.rationale: Atypical mycobacterial cervical adenitis is usually indolent, non-tender, in preschool children with a violaceous overly. (Source: RCH CPG: Cervical lymphadenopathy)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed when a child has fever for 5 days or more with 2-3 (rather than 4) of the principal clinical criteria plus a supportive laboratory panel pe.
key_points: Incomplete KD: fever plus 2-3 principal criteria plus supportive lab panel meets AHA treatment thres.
IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin is first-line; do not wait for coronary changes on echo.
Cervical adenitis unresponsive to antibiotics, without abscess on ultrasound, plus supportive labs,.
explanation.pearls: Sterile pyuria plus a cervical node without abscess on ultrasound plus a CRP over 100 in a child febrile past day 5 should prompt IVIG for incomplete Kawasaki d.

sources.label: AHA scientific statement on Kawasaki disease

subtopic_detail: Bilious vomiting in an infant - malrotation with midgut volvulus
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the emergency department to assess a 5 week old boy with three episodes of green vomiting in the last four hours. He was born at term and has been formula-fed since day 4 after breastfeeding did not establish. His mother reports that until today he has been feeding well with progressive weight gain. There has been no diarrhoea, no fever, no unwell contacts.

He cried inconsolably when the ambulance service placed the intravenous cannula, then became quiet, mottled and drowsy en route.

On examination he is pale, floppy and cool peripherally, with a tender-looking distended abdomen; capillary refill is four seconds and he is drowsy but rousable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178 /min, blood pressure 68/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 58 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.4 degC
data_table.Examination: Mottled infant, drowsy but rousable, distended and tender abdomen, no visible peristaltic wave, no palpable olive, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas pH 7.22, HCO3 14 mmol/L (22-26), lactate 5.8 mmol/L (<2), base excess -12, glucose 4.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Give 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus and arrange urgent upper GI contrast study before surgical referral
options.rationale: Bilious vomiting in an infant with shock is malrotation with midgut volvulus until surgically excluded. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting)

options.text: Perform bedside abdominal ultrasound to look for a pyloric olive before considering surgical referral
options.rationale: Pyloric stenosis causes non-bilious projectile vomiting because the obstruction is proximal to the ampulla of Vater. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

options.text: Trial oral rehydration solution 10 mL every ten minutes for two hours before any further investigations
options.rationale: Oral rehydration is contraindicated in a shocked drowsy infant with a surgical abdomen and bilious vomiting; aspiration. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Give intramuscular ceftriaxone empirically and arrange urgent lumbar puncture in the resuscitation bay
options.rationale: Sepsis is on the differential but the discriminating feature is bilious vomiting in an infant, which is a surgical emerg. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

options.text: Give 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus, insert nasogastric tube on free drainage, and phone paediatric surgery
options.rationale: Bilious vomiting plus shock in an infant is midgut volvulus complicating malrotation until proven otherwise, and the pri. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting)

explanation.summary: Bilious vomiting in an infant is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise; the feared diagnosis is malrotation with midgut volvulus, which can produce bowel necrosis within hour.
key_points: Bilious vomiting in an infant is malrotation with volvulus until surgically proven otherwise.
Shocked infant with bilious vomiting: resuscitate and phone surgery, do NOT go to radiology first.
NGT on free drainage decompresses the stomach and reduces vomiting risk.
explanation.pearls: A shocked infant with green vomit goes to theatre for Ladd's procedure, not to the contrast suite; upper GI series is only for the stable, uncertain case.

subtopic_detail: Bruising in a non-mobile infant
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4 month old girl in the emergency department. She has been brought by her mother's partner because she seemed 'off' and would not settle after her afternoon nap. Her mother is at work and could not be reached. The partner has been caring for the baby for two weeks.

On undressing you find a 1 cm yellow-brown bruise on the left cheek and a 2 cm bruise over the medial aspect of the right upper arm. The partner states 'she rolled off the couch onto a soft rug an hour ago' and thinks the arm bruise came from the car seat harness. The child is not yet rolling per the routine 4 month check last week.

Examination is otherwise normal with a soft anterior fontanelle, no scleral haemorrhage, no oral trauma, no bony tenderness on limb palpation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 /min, respiratory rate 34 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, appropriately interactive, well perfused, 1 cm yellow-brown cheek bruise, 2 cm medial upper arm bruise, no other cutaneous findings, no fractures palpable, anterior fontanelle soft
data_table.Investigations: Nil performed yet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Admit for a full non-accidental injury workup and notify state child protection with hospital social worker
options.rationale: Bruising in a non-mobile infant, with an inconsistent mechanism from a non-parent carer, meets criteria for a full NAI w. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Reassure the partner, arrange GP review in 48 hours, and document the bruises in the medical record
options.rationale: Bruising in a non-mobile infant carries a high probability of inflicted injury (TEN-4 rule: bruises in a child under 4 m. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Perform full blood count and coagulation studies only, and discharge home if these results are normal
options.rationale: A normal coagulation screen does not rule out inflicted injury; it forms one part of the NAI workup alongside skeletal s. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Confront the partner about inconsistency of story and refuse to release the child until police attend
options.rationale: Confrontation is not the doctor's role and may compromise the safety of the mother, the child, and staff. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Discharge to the mother when she arrives after she confirms the mechanism given by the current partner
options.rationale: Discharging on a second-hand confirmation of the mechanism does not add clinical information and does not discharge the. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

explanation.summary: Bruising in an infant who is not yet cruising is one of the strongest single features of inflicted injury.
key_points: Bruises in a pre-mobile infant are inflicted injury until otherwise explained.
TEN-4-FACES-p flags bruises requiring NAI workup: torso, ear, neck, or any in under-4-month-olds.
Structured workup: skeletal survey, fundoscopy, coagulation, CT head as indicated, social review.
explanation.pearls: The rule 'if they don't cruise, they don't bruise' means any bruise in an infant under 4 months mandates a full non-accidental injury workup plus notification t.

subtopic_detail: Paediatric DKA with subclinical cerebral oedema
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar caring for a 7 year old girl six hours into her admission for new-onset diabetic ketoacidosis. She presented with a two week history of polyuria, weight loss, and a two day history of vomiting and hyperventilation. Initial venous pH was 7.05, glucose 32 mmol/L, ketones 5.6 mmol/L, corrected sodium 143 mmol/L.

She received a 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus over 60 minutes and then commenced maintenance plus deficit fluids assuming an 8% dehydration at 5.5 mL/kg/h, with insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/h started one hour after fluids. On the current review her glucose has fallen from 32 to 12 mmol/L over the last four hours.

The nurse escalates because the child has become increasingly withdrawn over the last 45 minutes; she now complains of a headache, was briefly incontinent of urine, and has vomited once. Her father remarks she 'seems slower to answer' than at admission.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72 /min (was 132 on arrival), blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Neurological examination: GCS 13 (E4 V4 M5), pupils equal and reactive at 3 mm, no focal weakness, no papilloedema visible on bedside fundoscopy
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas pH 7.24 HCO3 14 mmol/L, glucose 12 mmol/L, sodium 141 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), ketones 3.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next intervention?

options.text: Add 5% glucose to the intravenous fluids and continue insulin at 0.05 units/kg/h without other change
options.rationale: Adding glucose is appropriate for the falling blood glucose (transitioning to two-bag or dextrose-added regimen once glu. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Give 3% saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg over 15 minutes, halve intravenous fluids, and escalate to PICU urgently
options.rationale: Falling heart rate with rising blood pressure (Cushing response), headache, vomiting, incontinence and GCS drop in a chi. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis; ISPAD DKA guideline)

options.text: Halt the insulin infusion for 30 minutes and reassess after correcting the potassium of 3.2 mmol/L
options.rationale: Interrupting insulin will halt ketolysis and worsen acidosis; potassium can be replaced through fluids while insulin con. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Give a 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus over 30 minutes to raise cerebral perfusion pressure now
options.rationale: Additional saline bolus can worsen cerebral oedema by continuing free-water accumulation intracellularly during rapid os. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Increase the insulin infusion to 0.1 units/kg/h to accelerate ketone clearance and neurological recovery
options.rationale: Insulin escalation would accelerate glucose fall, worsening osmolar shift and cerebral oedema, and is contraindicated du. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema complicates 0.5 to 1% of paediatric DKA episodes and carries around 20% mortality, with survivors often left with cognitive impairment.
key_points: Cushing response (bradycardia plus rising BP) plus GCS drop in DKA equals cerebral oedema until prov.
Give hyperosmolar therapy first (3% saline or mannitol); CT after stabilisation.
Halve IV fluid rate simultaneously.
explanation.pearls: 3% saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg over 15 minutes is the Australian first-line for suspected paediatric DKA cerebral oedema when a rising BP with falling pulse plus GCS.

subtopic_detail: Duct-dependent congenital heart disease presenting after nursery discharge
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 6 day old boy brought in by his parents because he has become mottled and off feeds over the last four hours. He was born at 39 weeks by uneventful vaginal delivery, passed the routine 24-hour saturation screen with pre-ductal SpO2 96% and post-ductal SpO2 95%, and was discharged at 48 hours. Feeding has been described as 'okay' until yesterday when volumes dropped.

Today he is grey, cool and lethargic. Femoral pulses are difficult to palpate; brachial pulses are volume-adequate. Precordium is quiet with no murmur audible. His liver is 3 cm below the costal margin.

A pre-ductal (right hand) SpO2 reads 84% and post-ductal (right foot) SpO2 reads 68% on room air.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 172 /min, blood pressure 62/34 mmHg (right arm), respiratory rate 68 /min, temperature 36.2 degC
data_table.Cardiovascular examination: Weak femoral pulses, strong brachial pulses, quiet precordium, no murmur, hepatomegaly 3 cm below costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas pH 7.14, HCO3 10 mmol/L, lactate 8.4 mmol/L (<2), sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, glucose 3.6 mmol/L, chest X-ray: mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette, normal pulmonary vascularity

lead_in: What is the single best immediate intervention?

options.text: Give a 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus over 20 minutes and repeat if perfusion does not improve
options.rationale: Volume in a duct-dependent left-sided obstruction (likely coarctation or interrupted aortic arch here) can worsen pulmon. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal collapse)

options.text: Intubate and ventilate with FiO2 1.0 to correct the hypoxia and hyperventilate for pulmonary vasodilatation
options.rationale: High FiO2 in duct-dependent left-sided obstruction is harmful because oxygen constricts the ductus and worsens systemic. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal collapse)

options.text: Commence intravenous prostaglandin E1 5 to 10 nanogram/kg/min and prepare for intubation if apnoea develops
options.rationale: Neonatal collapse in the first two weeks of life with weak femoral pulses, a pre-post-ductal saturation gradient greater. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal collapse)

options.text: Give intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg and lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg for suspected neonatal septic collapse
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics are reasonable while workup proceeds because sepsis is a differential, but delaying prostaglandin. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal collapse)

options.text: Give intramuscular adrenaline 10 microgram/kg and prepare for tension pneumothorax needle decompression
options.rationale: There is no clinical evidence of tension pneumothorax or anaphylaxis; the picture fits duct-dependent circulation. (Source: ANZCOR: Neonatal)

explanation.summary: Neonates with duct-dependent left-sided obstructions (critical coarctation, interrupted aortic arch, hypoplastic left heart, critical aortic stenosis) can pass 24-hour saturation s.
key_points: A ductal-arch obstruction can pass the 24-hour saturation screen; collapse comes days later.
Pre- to post-ductal SpO2 gradient greater than 3% with weak femorals equals duct-dependent CHD.
Prostaglandin E1 5-10 nanogram/kg/min reopens the ductus.
explanation.pearls: In a collapsed neonate under 2 weeks with pre-post-ductal saturation difference over 3% and weak femorals, start prostaglandin E1 at 5 nanogram/kg/min immediate.

subtopic_detail: PPH first uterotonic escalation
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite three minutes after a spontaneous vaginal delivery at 39 weeks. The mother is a 30 year old para 2 who laboured for eight hours; active management of the third stage was performed with 10 units intramuscular oxytocin at anterior shoulder delivery, and the placenta was delivered complete at four minutes. Her booking blood pressure was 118/72; there has been no antenatal hypertension.

The midwife reports estimated blood loss of 900 mL in the last two minutes, ongoing brisk trickle from the vaginal introitus, and a uterus that is soft to palpation above the umbilicus.

On your rapid review the mother is pale, alert, with brisk fresh vaginal bleeding and no perineal trauma visible on inspection. There is no calf swelling and no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Soft boggy uterus at umbilicus, brisk fresh vaginal bleeding, placenta appears complete on tray inspection, no perineal or vaginal wall trauma
data_table.Investigations: Bedside haemoglobin 96 g/L (115-160), venous access 16 gauge x 2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Repeat intramuscular oxytocin 10 units and continue bimanual uterine compression by the treating team
options.rationale: Escalation to a second-line uterotonic acting on a different receptor is more effective than repeating oxytocin. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Administer intramuscular carboprost 250 microgram, a synthetic prostaglandin F2 alpha, as next step
options.rationale: Carboprost is third-line in Australian sequencing (after oxytocin and ergometrine) because of significant bronchospasm,. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Administer misoprostol 800 microgram rectally as the immediate next uterotonic escalation step now
options.rationale: Misoprostol has a role when parenteral uterotonics are unavailable or ergot is contraindicated; it acts slowly (peak eff. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Give IV oxytocin 5 units by slow injection then infusion of 40 units over 4 hours plus ergometrine 250 microgram
options.rationale: Australian PPH sequencing: intravenous oxytocin bolus plus infusion escalates the initial uterotonic, and ergometrine (a. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement; AMH: Uterotonics)

options.text: Proceed to theatre for examination under anaesthesia before adding any further uterotonic escalation
options.rationale: Uterotonic escalation is done in parallel with examination under anaesthesia; deferring pharmacology until theatre waste. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

explanation.summary: Primary PPH management follows the four Ts (tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin) and a stepwise uterotonic ladder: oxytocin (intravenous bolus plus infusion) as first-line, ergometrine.
key_points: Tone first (uterine atony is the commonest cause) - massage plus escalating uterotonics.
Oxytocin first-line, ergometrine second unless hypertension/cardiac disease, carboprost third.
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of PPH onset (WOMAN trial).
explanation.pearls: Ergometrine 250 microgram intramuscularly is second-line PPH pharmacology only if the mother is normotensive and has no cardiac disease; it acts on alpha-adrene.

subtopic_detail: Contraception choice with heavy menstrual bleeding and migraine with aura
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 28 year old woman in a mid-morning appointment for contraception review and heavy periods. She is nulliparous, in a stable relationship, and wants effective contraception without pregnancy for at least three years. Her cycles are regular at 28 days with seven days of heavy flow soaking through pads at two hourly intervals for the first three days; ferritin is 12 microgram/L. She has migraine with aura roughly monthly since her mid-teens; her body mass index is 24; she does not smoke.

On direct enquiry she has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism, no breast or cervical cancer history, and no unexplained vaginal bleeding.

Cervical screening is up to date and normal; pelvic examination is unremarkable with a normal-size uterus and no adnexal mass.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: BMI 24, normal thyroid, non-tender abdomen, normal-size mobile anteverted uterus, no adnexal mass, cervix healthy
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-160), ferritin 12 microgram/L (30-200), TSH 1.4 mIU/L, urine hCG negative, recent HPV screen negative

lead_in: Which contraceptive option would you first recommend?

options.text: Progestogen-only pill norethisterone 350 microgram daily plus tranexamic acid during menstrual days
options.rationale: The traditional low-dose progestogen-only pill requires a three-hour dosing window and is user-dependent; it does not re. (Source: RANZCOG contraception)

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill with ethinyloestradiol 30 microgram plus levonorgestrel 150 microgram daily
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC category 4 (unacceptable risk) in migraine with aura at any age because of incr. (Source: RANZCOG contraception; UKMEC)

options.text: Copper intrauterine device with 10-year duration and no menstrual loss reduction benefit at all
options.rationale: The copper IUD is highly effective contraception but typically INCREASES menstrual blood loss and pain, and would worsen. (Source: RANZCOG contraception)

options.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscularly every 12 weeks with bone-density monitoring
options.rationale: Depot progestin is safe in migraine with aura and reduces bleeding, but bone mineral density falls with prolonged use an. (Source: RANZCOG contraception; AMH)

options.text: Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device 52 mg with 5-year duration and menstrual loss reduction
options.rationale: Levonorgestrel-releasing IUD is the most effective non-permanent contraception (failure under 0.2%) AND is first-line ho. (Source: RANZCOG contraception; Family Planning Alliance Australia)

explanation.summary: Migraine with aura is UKMEC category 4 for combined hormonal contraception because of increased ischaemic stroke risk.
key_points: Migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception.
LNG-IUD is first-line for heavy menstrual bleeding in Australia.
Copper IUD increases menstrual blood loss and worsens iron deficiency.
explanation.pearls: The 52 mg LNG-IUD reduces menstrual blood loss by about 90% at 12 months and rescues ferritin, all while providing the most effective reversible contraception.

subtopic_detail: Group B streptococcus intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis with unknown status
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 27 year old woman at 34 weeks and 2 days by dating scan with regular contractions every four minutes and ruptured membranes 30 minutes before arrival. This is her second pregnancy; the first was an uncomplicated term vaginal birth. Her antenatal care was fragmented and no group B streptococcus screening swab has been performed this pregnancy.

She has no penicillin allergy on direct questioning. Her observations are stable and she is afebrile. Foetal cardiotocography is reassuring with a baseline of 140/min, moderate variability and accelerations. Cervical examination confirms 4 cm dilatation with clear liquor.

Her first-child pregnancy did not include GBS screening either; that child was born at term without early-onset neonatal GBS disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Foetal: CTG baseline 140 /min, moderate variability, accelerations present, no decelerations
data_table.Investigations: White cells 12.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), CRP 4 mg/L (<5), high vaginal swab has NOT been performed this pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management with respect to group B streptococcus?

options.text: Commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g every four hours until birth of the baby
options.rationale: Preterm labour at 34 weeks with unknown GBS status meets the Australian risk-based indication for intrapartum antibiotic. (Source: RANZCOG GBS statement)

options.text: Take a high vaginal swab now and hold intrapartum antibiotics until the culture result returns after birth
options.rationale: Cultures take 24-48 hours; delaying antibiotics until results arrive misses the intrapartum window in preterm labour. (Source: RANZCOG GBS statement)

options.text: Do not give intrapartum antibiotics because she is afebrile, CRP is normal, and her prior child had no disease
options.rationale: Preterm labour under 37 weeks with unknown GBS status is a stand-alone indication for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG GBS statement)

options.text: Commence intravenous ampicillin 2 g loading then 1 g every four hours plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg once daily
options.rationale: This is empirical intra-amniotic infection therapy, not GBS prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG GBS statement)

options.text: Give a single dose of oral azithromycin 1 g orally in the birth suite as intrapartum GBS prophylaxis today
options.rationale: Azithromycin is used in caesarean labour antibiotic prophylaxis (with cefazolin) to reduce endometritis, not for GBS pro. (Source: RANZCOG GBS statement)

explanation.summary: Australian GBS prophylaxis uses a risk-based approach when universal screening at 35 to 37 weeks is unavailable or the woman presents in preterm labour.
key_points: Preterm labour under 37 weeks with unknown GBS status triggers empirical intrapartum prophylaxis.
Benzylpenicillin 3 g IV load then 1.8 g q4h until birth; cefazolin if non-severe penicillin allergy.
Clindamycin only for severe penicillin allergy AND documented clindamycin-susceptible GBS isolate.
explanation.pearls: Benzylpenicillin 1.8 g intravenously every 4 hours for at least 4 hours pre-delivery is the Australian GBS prophylaxis window that meaningfully reduces neonatal.

subtopic_detail: Antepartum haemorrhage with foetal exsanguination pattern
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite for a 32 year old primigravida at 37 weeks and 3 days. She reports a sudden gush of vaginal fluid at home 20 minutes ago that appeared blood-stained, followed by cessation of foetal movements. She was well until the event. Her routine anomaly scan noted a low-lying placenta with a bilobed morphology and a single-vessel cord; a follow-up scan at 32 weeks reported the placenta had migrated away from the internal os.

She is haemodynamically stable and denies pain. Speculum examination shows a small pool of blood-stained liquor in the vaginal vault and a closed cervix with no active bleeding.

Cardiotocography is being applied as you arrive.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Foetal: CTG baseline 88 /min, reduced variability, sinusoidal pattern
data_table.Investigations: Bedside haemoglobin (maternal) 132 g/L, Kleihauer-Betke result pending, coagulation studies normal

lead_in: What is the single best next step?

options.text: Trial of labour with continuous CTG monitoring given the maternal haemodynamic stability and painless bleed
options.rationale: Foetal bradycardia with sinusoidal pattern indicates foetal hypovolaemia and severe anaemia. Labour will lose the baby. (Source: RANZCOG antepartum haemorrhage)

options.text: Category 1 emergency caesarean section with paediatric team briefed for neonatal resuscitation and transfusion
options.rationale: Foetal bradycardia with sinusoidal pattern after painless ruptured membranes with blood-stained liquor is vasa praevia w. (Source: RANZCOG antepartum haemorrhage)

options.text: Arrange urgent bedside ultrasound to localise the placenta before deciding on mode of delivery in birth suite
options.rationale: Ultrasound wastes the survival window in vasa praevia with active exsanguination. (Source: RANZCOG antepartum haemorrhage)

options.text: Give intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg for foetal lung maturity and admit for observation before delivery
options.rationale: Corticosteroids do not treat foetal exsanguination and 37 weeks is past the routine steroid window. Delivery cannot wait. (Source: RANZCOG antepartum haemorrhage)

options.text: Perform emergency artificial rupture of membranes to accelerate delivery vaginally in the birth suite now
options.rationale: Membranes are already ruptured and the foetal circulation is compromised. (Source: RANZCOG antepartum haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia is unprotected foetal vessels crossing the internal os, either overlying a velamentous cord insertion (Type I) or between lobes of a bilobed or succenturiate placenta.
key_points: Vasa praevia: painless antepartum haemorrhage at rupture PLUS sinusoidal or bradycardic CTG.
Category 1 caesarean within 30 minutes; delay costs the baby.
Neonate needs immediate resuscitation and blood transfusion for anaemia.
explanation.pearls: A sinusoidal CTG with painless blood-stained liquor after membrane rupture is vasa praevia foetal exsanguination; the baby is born by category 1 caesarean and t.

subtopic_detail: Pre-eclampsia with severe features and magnesium sulfate indication
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33 year old primigravida at 33 weeks and 5 days admitted from clinic for further assessment of hypertension. Her booking blood pressure was 108/68 and she was previously well; there is no personal or family history of hypertension. Today at clinic her blood pressure was 168/108 on two readings 15 minutes apart. She reports a frontal headache since yesterday morning and mild epigastric discomfort described as heartburn.

On examination her tendon reflexes are brisk with two beats of ankle clonus. There is mild pitting pedal oedema. Foetal cardiotocography shows a reassuring baseline of 138/min with moderate variability and accelerations.

Proteinuria on dipstick is 3+; a random protein-to-creatinine ratio is 82 mg/mmol.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 168/108 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Foetal: CTG baseline 138 /min, moderate variability, accelerations, no decelerations
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-160), platelets 82 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 148 U/L (<40), creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90), urate 0.41 mmol/L, urine protein-to-creatinine 82 mg/mmol, LDH 620 U/L (<250), coagulation within normal limits, blood film without schistocytes

lead_in: In addition to antihypertensive control and planning delivery, what is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Administer intravenous hydralazine 5 mg boluses every 15 minutes for blood pressure control, no magnesium
options.rationale: Antihypertensive control is essential but does not prevent eclamptic seizures; magnesium is a separate pharmacological i. (Source: RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy)

options.text: Commence intravenous diazepam 5 mg for seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia and reassess in one hour
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are not first-line seizure prophylaxis in pre-eclampsia; magnesium sulfate is superior for eclamptic sei. (Source: RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy)

options.text: Commence magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenously over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion for at least 24 hours
options.rationale: Pre-eclampsia with severe features (BP >=160/110, headache, epigastric pain, platelets <100, ALT >2x normal, hyperreflex. (Source: RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy)

options.text: Administer intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg and defer any further intervention pending steroid completion
options.rationale: Betamethasone is indicated for foetal lung maturity at this gestation, but administering steroids without magnesium sulf. (Source: RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy)

options.text: Give aspirin 150 mg orally to reduce placental thromboxane production and delay progression of pre-eclampsia
options.rationale: Low-dose aspirin is preventive (started before 16 weeks in women at high risk); it has no acute role once pre-eclampsia. (Source: RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia is defined by any of BP >=160/110, thrombocytopaenia (platelets <100), impaired liver function (transaminases twice upper limit), progressive renal insufficien.
key_points: Severe pre-eclampsia criteria include BP >=160/110 OR end-organ features (platelets <100, ALT >2x no.
Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV load then 1 g/h reduces eclamptic seizures (MAGPIE).
Continue magnesium 24 hours after delivery or last seizure.
explanation.pearls: Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour is the Australian first-line for seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia; continue for 24 hours post-.

subtopic_detail: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome - moderate outpatient vs admission
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 30 year old woman referred by her fertility unit five days after transvaginal oocyte retrieval. She had 21 oocytes retrieved and her human chorionic gonadotropin trigger was a full agonist replacement rather than recombinant hCG, and she has not yet had embryo transfer. She reports abdominal distension, mild dyspnoea when lying flat, and reduced urine output.

On examination her abdomen is distended, non-tender, with shifting dullness but no guarding. Her weight is up 3.5 kg from oocyte retrieval baseline. Chest expansion is symmetrical with dullness at the right base.

Her body mass index is 22 and she is otherwise well. Bedside ultrasound shows large multi-follicular ovaries (right 12 cm, left 11 cm) and moderate ascites; a small right pleural effusion is noted on chest X-ray.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 /min, blood pressure 108/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen with shifting dullness, no guarding, dullness right lung base
data_table.Investigations: Haematocrit 46% (36-46), white cells 14.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), sodium 130 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), coagulation within normal limits, urine hCG negative

lead_in: What is the single best next step in management?

options.text: Discharge with outpatient monitoring, oral fluid intake targets and next-day fertility unit review appointment
options.rationale: Rising haematocrit (46%), hyponatraemia (130), oliguria on history, pleural effusion, weight gain >3 kg, dyspnoea and ta. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS statement)

options.text: Perform urgent bilateral ovarian cystectomy to reduce ovarian volume and third-space losses in the acute phase
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for ovarian torsion, cyst rupture with haemodynamic instability, or ectopic pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS statement)

options.text: Give a 500 mL 0.45% saline bolus and start furosemide 40 mg intravenously to correct oedema and third-spacing
options.rationale: Diuresis in OHSS is contraindicated while patients are intravascularly deplete (rising haematocrit, third-space losses). (Source: RANZCOG OHSS statement)

options.text: Admit for IV crystalloid, prophylactic enoxaparin, daily haematocrit, and paracentesis if respiratory decline
options.rationale: Moderate to severe OHSS is a high-VTE-risk state (haemoconcentration, oestradiol effect, immobility) and requires admiss. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS statement; RCOG green-top guideline)

options.text: Give a single intramuscular dose of dexamethasone 8 mg to reduce vascular permeability and third-space losses
options.rationale: Corticosteroids have not shown clinically important benefit in OHSS and are not standard therapy. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS statement)

explanation.summary: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome ranges from mild (self-limiting) to critical (respiratory failure, thrombosis, acute renal failure).
key_points: OHSS is a hypercoagulable, haemoconcentrated, third-space-loss state.
Admission for moderate to severe disease; VTE prophylaxis with LMWH.
Crystalloid volume replacement guided by haematocrit and urine output.
explanation.pearls: In moderate OHSS with haematocrit above 45%, isotonic crystalloid resuscitation plus VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin is the Australian standard; diuretics and h.

subtopic_detail: Amniotic fluid embolism with cardiorespiratory collapse and DIC
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite when the midwife calls you emergently to bay 4. A 38 year old para 3 delivered vaginally 12 minutes ago at 40 weeks after a two hour second stage; the placenta was delivered complete at seven minutes with routine oxytocin. She had felt breathless and 'panicked' immediately after the birth, coughed twice, then became agitated, then unresponsive.

On arrival she has agonal breathing, pulse is impalpable at the femoral, and there is torrential fresh vaginal bleeding from a soft boggy uterus and oozing from her cannula sites and speculum-untouched perineum.

CPR has been commenced by the midwife with 30:2. IV access is already available.

data_table.Vital signs: Impalpable central pulse, SpO2 unrecordable, agonal breaths, GCS 3
data_table.Examination: Soft boggy uterus, torrential vaginal bleeding, bleeding from cannula and perineum, no obvious trauma
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care haemoglobin 74 g/L, fibrinogen 0.8 g/L (2.0-4.5), platelets 62 x10^9/L, INR 2.4

lead_in: What is the single best pattern of immediate management?

options.text: Administer thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg intravenously since pulmonary embolism is the likely mechanism here
options.rationale: Thrombolysis in a bleeding coagulopathic patient is contraindicated and worsens haemorrhage. (Source: RCOG green-top AFE)

options.text: Give 500 mL crystalloid bolus, single ergometrine 250 microgram IM, and defer massive transfusion for 20 minutes
options.rationale: This underuses balanced blood products in a coagulopathic obstetric collapse and gives ergometrine (contraindicated in c. (Source: RANZCOG obstetric emergencies)

options.text: Prioritise B-Lynch suture in theatre without perimortem caesarean, continuing chest compressions during transfer
options.rationale: Perimortem caesarean is the priority to restore maternal cardiac output; B-Lynch is a specific tone-focused surgical tec. (Source: ANZCOR adult ALS)

options.text: Give recombinant activated factor VIIa 90 microgram/kg first-line to reverse coagulopathy before red cell transfusion
options.rationale: Recombinant factor VIIa is not a first-line agent for obstetric haemorrhage or AFE; balanced red cells, plasma, platelet. (Source: NBA patient blood management)

options.text: Continue ALS with left uterine displacement, activate massive transfusion 4:4:1, tranexamic acid, perimortem caesarean
options.rationale: Amniotic fluid embolism with cardiovascular collapse plus coagulopathy is the diagnosis and requires simultaneous cardio. (Source: RANZCOG obstetric emergencies; ANZCOR)

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare, catastrophic obstetric emergency presenting within minutes of labour, delivery or the immediate postpartum with hypoxia, hypotension, arrest and.
key_points: AFE: sudden peripartum collapse plus coagulopathy plus bleeding from puncture sites.
Massive transfusion protocol with 4:4:1 red cells:plasma:platelets and cryoprecipitate for fibrinoge.
Perimortem caesarean by 4 minutes of maternal arrest.
explanation.pearls: In a peripartum collapse with coagulopathy activate massive transfusion protocol at 4:4:1 and cryoprecipitate to keep fibrinogen above 2 g/L, and prepare for pe.

subtopic_detail: Uterine rupture during trial of labour after caesarean
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite reviewing a 34 year old para 1 at 40 weeks and 4 days who is undergoing a trial of labour after a previous lower segment caesarean section for breech at term. Labour was induced with an oxytocin infusion four hours ago after spontaneous rupture of membranes with clear liquor at admission. Her cervix was 5 cm at review one hour ago; contractions have been every three minutes.

The midwife has escalated because the mother has a sudden change: contractions have paused for three minutes, and the mother reports a burning sensation across her lower abdomen 'unlike the earlier pain'. The cardiotocograph baseline has fallen from 138 to 72 /min over 90 seconds and is not recovering.

On examination the presenting part is no longer palpable at 0 station on vaginal examination (previously station 0); abdominal palpation reveals an easily palpated foetal part in the maternal upper abdomen.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Foetal: CTG baseline 72 /min for 90 seconds with reduced variability and no recovery
data_table.Examination: Presenting part no longer engaged, easily palpable foetal parts in maternal upper abdomen

lead_in: What is the single best immediate management?

options.text: Cease oxytocin, give terbutaline 250 microgram subcutaneously, and mobilise category 1 caesarean team
options.rationale: Sudden change in pain character, loss of station, palpable foetal parts abdominally and prolonged foetal bradycardia in. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC; RCOG green-top VBAC)

options.text: Continue the oxytocin infusion and reassess after another two contractions with fresh CTG interpretation
options.rationale: Uterine rupture requires immediate cessation of oxytocin (which contributes to rupture through hyperstimulation) and cat. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

options.text: Perform intrauterine resuscitation with left lateral position, IV fluid bolus and oxygen; reassess in 10 minutes
options.rationale: Intrauterine resuscitation is appropriate for reversible foetal decelerations without rupture features. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

options.text: Prepare for instrumental vaginal delivery with rotational forceps when the next contraction pattern resumes
options.rationale: Instrumental delivery from station 0 with an unrestored contraction pattern and possible ruptured uterus is not feasible. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

options.text: Give ergometrine 250 microgram intramuscularly to restore uterine tone and reassess bleeding in 10 minutes
options.rationale: Ergometrine increases uterine contraction and worsens rupture; it is a postpartum agent, not an intrapartum one. (Source: AMH: Uterotonics)

explanation.summary: Uterine rupture in a trial of labour after caesarean carries substantial maternal and perinatal mortality.
key_points: VBAC uterine rupture: sudden pain change, loss of station, palpable foetal parts, prolonged bradycar.
Immediate: cease oxytocin, tocolysis, category 1 caesarean.
Ergometrine is intrapartum-contraindicated in this scenario.
explanation.pearls: In a suspected uterine rupture during VBAC, terbutaline 250 microgram subcutaneously buys transfer time to theatre; category 1 caesarean is the definitive step.

subtopic_detail: Second-generation antipsychotic metabolic monitoring
stem:
You are the community mental health registrar seeing a 28 year old man who was commenced on olanzapine 15 mg nightly six months ago after a first-episode psychosis. He has been adherent, has had no relapse, and is enrolled in an early psychosis service. He now describes low energy, snoring witnessed by his partner, and a 9 kg weight gain since commencement.

His pre-treatment weight was 78 kg (BMI 24); his weight today is 87 kg (BMI 27). His fasting bloods this week show glucose 6.4 mmol/L, total cholesterol 6.1 mmol/L with LDL 4.0 mmol/L and triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L, and HbA1c 44 mmol/mol.

He describes his mental state as stable with residual mild negative symptoms; he lives with his partner and has re-started a plumbing apprenticeship.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: BMI 27, waist circumference 102 cm, no thyroid enlargement
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), HbA1c 44 mmol/mol (<42 non-diabetic), total cholesterol 6.1 mmol/L, LDL 4.0 mmol/L, HDL 0.9 mmol/L, triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L, ALT 42 U/L, TSH 1.6 mIU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Continue olanzapine unchanged, refer to a community dietitian, and set a review appointment for six months time
options.rationale: Watchful waiting alone does not address progressive metabolic risk in the highest-risk agent (olanzapine and clozapine c. (Source: RANZCP guidelines; eTG: Psychotropic)

options.text: Discuss switching to aripiprazole or a lower-metabolic-risk antipsychotic and start metformin plus lifestyle programme
options.rationale: Olanzapine carries the highest metabolic risk of the second-generation antipsychotics. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)

options.text: Add a low dose of an atypical antipsychotic like risperidone to allow olanzapine dose reduction over three months
options.rationale: Antipsychotic polypharmacy is not evidence-based for adjusting metabolic tolerability; risperidone still contributes to. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)

options.text: Prescribe a moderate-intensity statin now to treat dyslipidaemia and continue olanzapine at the current dose
options.rationale: A statin addresses one component but leaves the underlying drug driver of weight gain, prediabetes and dyslipidaemia in. (Source: NHFA CVD prevention)

options.text: Cease olanzapine abruptly and monitor for return of psychotic symptoms with weekly community mental health review
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of antipsychotic after first-episode psychosis risks relapse; a cross-titration to a lower-risk agent m. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)

explanation.summary: Second-generation antipsychotics differ substantially in metabolic risk (clozapine and olanzapine highest; quetiapine and risperidone intermediate; aripiprazole, ziprasidone and lu.
key_points: Olanzapine and clozapine are the highest-metabolic-risk antipsychotics.
Metabolic monitoring at baseline, 6 weeks, 3 months, then annually.
Metformin reduces antipsychotic-induced weight gain by around 3 kg.
explanation.pearls: Weight gain over 7% of baseline on olanzapine triggers active intervention: metformin, structured lifestyle, or switch to aripiprazole - not watchful waiting.

subtopic_detail: Alcohol withdrawal seizure prophylaxis in general medical ward
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 44 year old man to the general medical ward after presenting to the emergency department with 12 hours of coarse tremor, sweating, nausea and one episode of vomiting. He is a mechanic with a long-standing pattern of drinking eight standard drinks daily; his last drink was 18 hours ago when he 'decided to stop' after his wife left. He has had two previous withdrawal seizures during unmedicated abstinence attempts but has never had delirium tremens.

He is agitated but oriented. His current Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol - revised score is 18. Vital signs are stable. Bedside blood glucose is 5.8 mmol/L. He denies suicidal ideation and does not report visual or auditory hallucinations.

He has no known liver disease, no benzodiazepine dependence, and no chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 /min, blood pressure 148/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.1 degC
data_table.Examination: Coarse tremor bilaterally, diaphoretic, oriented, no asterixis, no jaundice, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 5.8 mmol/L, ALT 58 U/L, GGT 145 U/L, INR 1.1, platelets 168 x10^9/L, thiamine yet to be given

lead_in: What is the single best next step?

options.text: Give oral thiamine 100 mg daily and observe without benzodiazepine because he is oriented at the moment
options.rationale: A CIWA-Ar of 18 is moderate to severe withdrawal with prior seizures; withholding benzodiazepines risks seizure and prog. (Source: eTG: Alcohol withdrawal)

options.text: Give oral chlordiazepoxide 25 mg every 6 hours on a fixed schedule for 5 days regardless of symptom pattern
options.rationale: Symptom-triggered dosing outperforms fixed-schedule dosing in reducing total benzodiazepine load and length of stay. (Source: eTG: Alcohol withdrawal)

options.text: Commence oral diazepam 20 mg every 2 hours titrated to CIWA-Ar plus parenteral thiamine 300 mg IV first dose
options.rationale: Symptom-triggered benzodiazepine loading (diazepam 20 mg oral every 2 hours until CIWA-Ar <10) is the Australian standar. (Source: eTG: Alcohol withdrawal; RACP alcohol guidelines)

options.text: Commence phenytoin 15 mg/kg intravenous load and lorazepam 1 mg intramuscularly as seizure prophylaxis today
options.rationale: Phenytoin does not prevent alcohol withdrawal seizures because the pathophysiology is GABA receptor rebound, not the mec. (Source: eTG: Alcohol withdrawal)

options.text: Start clonidine 150 microgram three times daily to control autonomic features without any benzodiazepine
options.rationale: Alpha-2 agonists mask autonomic features but do not prevent seizures or delirium; they should not replace benzodiazepine. (Source: eTG: Alcohol withdrawal)

explanation.summary: Alcohol withdrawal severity is scored with CIWA-Ar; a score of 15 or more is moderate to severe and needs inpatient management with benzodiazepine loading.
key_points: CIWA-Ar over 15 is moderate to severe withdrawal - inpatient benzodiazepine loading.
Diazepam 20 mg oral every 2 hours titrated until CIWA-Ar <10 (Australian standard).
Parenteral thiamine 300 mg IV three times daily for 3-5 days BEFORE any glucose.
explanation.pearls: In Australian alcohol withdrawal protocols, diazepam 20 mg oral loading every 2 hours titrated to CIWA-Ar is the seizure-preventing regimen; thiamine 300 mg IV.

subtopic_detail: Lithium initiation pre-treatment workup
stem:
You are the community mental health registrar reviewing a 32 year old woman with bipolar I disorder recovering from her third manic episode. She has been managed with olanzapine and lorazepam during admission and is now stable on olanzapine 10 mg nightly. She wants to change to a longer-term mood stabiliser and is not pregnant, not planning pregnancy in the next 12 months, and uses a copper intrauterine device. She has no diagnosed cardiac or thyroid disease.

She is otherwise well with no NSAID or ACE inhibitor use. She works as an accountant with regular access to routine bloods. Her BMI is 24 and her blood pressure is 118/72.

After discussion of options, she prefers lithium given the family history of bipolar disorder that responded well to lithium.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Examination: BMI 24, no goitre, no oedema, cardiovascular examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free T4 within normal limits, creatinine 68 micromol/L, eGFR >90 mL/min, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L, urine hCG negative

lead_in: Which of the following investigations is the single most important to complete before commencing lithium?

options.text: Baseline 12-lead electrocardiogram to exclude conduction abnormalities before starting lithium therapy
options.rationale: An ECG is recommended before lithium initiation for patients over 40 or with cardiac risk factors, but it is not the hig. (Source: eTG: Psychotropic)

options.text: Baseline liver function tests including ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, bilirubin and albumin before commencement
options.rationale: Lithium is renally cleared and not hepatically metabolised; LFTs are not part of the routine pre-lithium workup. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

options.text: Fasting glucose plus lipid profile including total cholesterol, LDL, HDL and triglycerides before commencement
options.rationale: These are relevant to second-generation antipsychotics rather than lithium; they are not part of the lithium pre-treatme. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

options.text: Pregnancy test plus baseline UEC, thyroid function and calcium documenting adherence to reliable contraception
options.rationale: Lithium is teratogenic (Ebstein anomaly with first-trimester exposure; historical risk about 1 in 1000, higher than base. (Source: eTG: Psychotropic; AMH: Lithium)

options.text: Anti-thyroid antibodies including anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin to identify latent autoimmune thyroid disease
options.rationale: Anti-thyroid antibodies are not part of the routine pre-lithium screen; baseline TSH is. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

explanation.summary: Pre-lithium workup includes urea, electrolytes, creatinine and eGFR, thyroid function (TSH and free T4), corrected calcium, pregnancy test in women of reproductive age, and baselin.
key_points: Baseline pre-lithium: UEC, TSH, calcium, pregnancy test, ECG if over 40 or cardiac history.
Lithium is teratogenic - Ebstein anomaly in first trimester; reliable contraception required.
Monitor lithium level, renal function, TSH and calcium every 6 months.
explanation.pearls: Before starting lithium in a woman of reproductive age, confirm negative pregnancy test and reliable contraception; Ebstein anomaly risk is around 1 in 1000 wit.

subtopic_detail: Catatonia in acute psychiatric setting
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar called to the acute psychiatric inpatient unit to review a 24 year old man with schizoaffective disorder who has become progressively unwell over 24 hours. He was admitted a week ago for a psychotic relapse and started on risperidone 3 mg twice daily. Over the last day he has stopped eating and speaking and is now mute, staring past the interviewer.

On examination he holds his right arm in a raised position when you gently lift it, maintaining the posture for over a minute after you withdraw your hand. He resists passive movement with equal counter-force ('gegenhalten') and grimaces intermittently. There is no tremor and no lead-pipe rigidity.

His observations show mild tachycardia; he is afebrile.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 /min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.0 degC
data_table.Examination: Waxy flexibility, gegenhalten, mutism, staring, negativism (turning away from food), Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale score 16
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 220 U/L (<200), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), calcium and magnesium within normal limits, urine drug screen negative, blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the single best next step?

options.text: Continue risperidone, add haloperidol 5 mg intramuscularly, and reassess response within the next hour
options.rationale: Escalating antipsychotic dosing in catatonia risks neuroleptic malignant syndrome (which shares the catatonia phenotype. (Source: RANZCP acute behavioural disturbance)

options.text: Refer immediately for electroconvulsive therapy without a lorazepam trial or diagnostic challenge
options.rationale: ECT is definitive for benzodiazepine-refractory catatonia or malignant catatonia; lorazepam trial precedes ECT because m. (Source: RANZCP ECT guideline)

options.text: Start dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg intravenously for suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome with rigidity
options.rationale: NMS is on the differential but this patient is afebrile with mild tachycardia and CK 220; the phenotype (waxy flexibilit. (Source: RANZCP acute behavioural disturbance)

options.text: Trial olanzapine 10 mg intramuscularly and escalate second-generation antipsychotic sedation dosing
options.rationale: Second-generation antipsychotic sedation does not treat catatonia and can worsen it, potentially precipitating NMS in an. (Source: RANZCP acute behavioural disturbance)

options.text: Give a test dose of lorazepam 1 to 2 mg intramuscularly and reassess response over 10 to 15 minutes
options.rationale: A lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IM or IV) is diagnostic and therapeutic in catatonia; around 60-80% of catatonia responds. (Source: RANZCP acute behavioural disturbance; StatPearls Catatonia)

explanation.summary: Catatonia presents with mutism, staring, waxy flexibility, gegenhalten, negativism, posturing, echolalia or echopraxia, and can arise in mood disorders, psychotic disorders, and me.
key_points: Catatonia: mutism, waxy flexibility, gegenhalten, negativism, posturing, echo phenomena.
Lorazepam 1-2 mg is diagnostic and therapeutic within 15 minutes.
Malignant catatonia has fever and autonomic dysregulation; overlaps with NMS.
explanation.pearls: A single intramuscular test dose of lorazepam 1 to 2 mg both diagnoses catatonia and treats it in about 70% of cases within 15 minutes; refractory cases proceed.

subtopic_detail: Valproate in women of reproductive age
stem:
You are the community mental health registrar seeing a 26 year old woman with bipolar I disorder who has had two hospital admissions for mania. She has failed adequate trials of lithium and olanzapine (poor efficacy and metabolic weight gain respectively). Her psychiatrist is considering valproate as the next mood stabiliser. She is sexually active with her male partner, uses condoms only, and has not made pregnancy plans.

She has no personal history of neural tube defects and no family history of open spina bifida. Baseline liver function and platelet count are normal. She has been counselled that condom-only use has around a 15% typical-use annual failure rate.

She would prefer to try valproate but wants to explore what safety framework applies.

data_table.Examination: BMI 26, no goitre, no oedema, cardiovascular examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: ALT 22 U/L, platelets 268 x10^9/L, INR 1.0, urine hCG negative

lead_in: What is the single best next step?

options.text: Establish highly effective LARC contraception plus signed annual acknowledgement, then commence valproate
options.rationale: The valproate pregnancy prevention framework requires documented highly effective contraception (LARC preferred, or two. (Source: TGA valproate advisory; RANZCP mood disorders guideline)

options.rationale: Australian and international guidance (TGA and MHRA valproate pregnancy prevention programme) require documented highly. (Source: TGA valproate advisory; RANZCP mood disorders guideline)

options.rationale: Carbamazepine is also teratogenic (neural tube defects, craniofacial abnormalities) and induces oestrogen metabolism, re. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline)

options.rationale: Lamotrigine has a more favourable teratogenic profile but is a poor choice for acute mania prevention; it is more effect. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline)
