options.rationale: Valproate is not absolutely contraindicated in women of reproductive age in Australia; it can be used inside the pregnan. (Source: TGA valproate advisory)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is teratogenic with a 30-40% risk of congenital malformations and neurodevelopmental impairment (major malformations 10%, IQ reduction of about 8 points, autism sp.
key_points: Valproate: 30-40% congenital malformation and neurodevelopmental risk in pregnancy.
Pregnancy prevention programme with LARC or dual method contraception before initiation.
Annual specialist re-consent with signed acknowledgement.
explanation.pearls: In Australia valproate is only started in a woman of reproductive age with a levonorgestrel-IUD or implant in situ (or dual method), signed annual re-consent, a.

subtopic_detail: SSRI discontinuation vs depression relapse
stem:
You are the general practitioner registrar seeing a 38 year old woman five days after she stopped her paroxetine 20 mg daily. She had been on paroxetine for 14 months for a moderate major depressive episode that fully remitted after six weeks; she stopped the medication herself on advice from a friend who felt she had 'been on it long enough'. Her last dose was five days ago.

Since then she describes new brief lightning-like sensations down her arms and legs on turning her head ('electric shocks'), vivid dreams, mild nausea, dizziness on standing, and a low-grade flu-like sensation. Her partner reports she is a bit irritable but not tearful or withdrawn. She is sleeping.

Her mood examination reveals a normal-range mood, appropriate reactivity, no anhedonia, no suicidal ideation, and no hopelessness.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg (no significant postural drop), respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, normal affective range, no psychomotor slowing, no anhedonia, no suicidality, no hopelessness

lead_in: What is the single best next step?

options.text: Diagnose major depressive relapse and increase the paroxetine dose to 30 mg daily with review in two weeks
options.rationale: There is no depressive relapse: mood is euthymic, no anhedonia, no suicidal ideation, and symptoms are physical rather t. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline)

options.text: Restart paroxetine 20 mg daily and plan a slow taper over 8 to 12 weeks with a fluoxetine bridge if needed
options.rationale: The symptom cluster (electric shock sensations, vivid dreams, dizziness, flu-like, irritability - the FINISH mnemonic) p. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline; RCPsych stopping antidepressants)

options.text: Prescribe a benzodiazepine short-term for the anxiety-like symptoms and reassess response in two weeks time
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines mask discontinuation symptoms without treating the underlying serotonergic rebound; they add dependence. (Source: eTG: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add lithium as an augmentation agent for treatment-resistant depression despite prior full remission on paroxetine
options.rationale: There is no evidence of treatment-resistant depression; the depression fully remitted on paroxetine. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline)

options.text: Advise ongoing abstinence and predict resolution within 5 days regardless of severity or symptom duration
options.rationale: Ongoing abstinence with severe discontinuation symptoms is unnecessarily punishing, and paroxetine's short half-life oft. (Source: RCPsych stopping antidepressants)

explanation.summary: Antidepressant discontinuation syndrome affects up to 20-30% of people stopping SSRIs, most commonly with short-half-life agents (paroxetine, venlafaxine).
key_points: FINISH mnemonic: flu-like, insomnia, nausea, imbalance, sensory, hyperarousal.
Paroxetine, venlafaxine, duloxetine have highest discontinuation burden.
Distinguish from depressive relapse: mood is euthymic in discontinuation.
explanation.pearls: Electric-shock sensations plus a euthymic mood after stopping paroxetine is discontinuation syndrome, not relapse; restart and slow-taper over 8-12 weeks.

subtopic_detail: Uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant adult woman
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 32 year old woman with two days of dysuria and urinary frequency. She has had three previous urinary tract infections in her lifetime, most recently 18 months ago, all uncomplicated and community-acquired. She is not pregnant, is not immunocompromised, has no diabetes, and has no history of pyelonephritis or renal tract abnormality.

She denies fever, flank pain, nausea, and vomiting. There has been no recent overseas travel and no recent hospitalisation. She has no drug allergies.

On examination her observations are within normal limits; the abdomen is soft with mild suprapubic tenderness and no flank tenderness. Bedside urinalysis is nitrite positive with 3+ leukocyte esterase.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72 /min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused, mild suprapubic tenderness, no flank tenderness, no vaginal discharge
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis nitrite positive, leukocytes 3+, urine microscopy and culture sent, urine hCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic?

options.text: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally twice daily for 3 days as empirical first-line for uncomplicated cystitis
options.rationale: Fluoroquinolones are reserved for complicated infections, resistance, or intolerance in Australian empirical UTI pathway. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic; TGA fluoroquinolone advisory)

options.text: Amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times daily for 5 days as empirical first-line for uncomplicated cystitis
options.rationale: Amoxicillin has high resistance in Australian E coli isolates (about 40-50%) and is not an empirical first-line for cyst. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)

options.text: Trimethoprim 300 mg orally at night for 3 days OR nitrofurantoin 100 mg 6-hourly for 5 days
options.rationale: Australian eTG first-line for uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant women without risk factors is trimethoprim 300 mg n. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)

options.text: Cefalexin 500 mg orally 6-hourly for 5 days as empirical first-line therapy for uncomplicated cystitis
options.rationale: Cefalexin is second-line where trimethoprim resistance is documented or first-line agents are contraindicated; it is bro. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)

options.text: Fosfomycin 3 g single oral dose as empirical first-line therapy for uncomplicated community cystitis
options.rationale: Fosfomycin is available in Australia via the Special Access Scheme for multidrug-resistant uncomplicated cystitis; it is. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant women without immune compromise, renal tract abnormality, or recent healthcare exposure is treated empirically without waiting for culture.
key_points: First-line uncomplicated cystitis: trimethoprim 3 days OR nitrofurantoin 5 days.
Amoxicillin has too much E coli resistance to be empirical.
Fluoroquinolones and cefalexin are reserved for resistance or intolerance.
explanation.pearls: Australian empirical uncomplicated cystitis therapy is trimethoprim 300 mg nightly for 3 days, or nitrofurantoin 100 mg 6-hourly for 5 days; culture is sent but.

subtopic_detail: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes
stem:
You are the medical registrar covering the renal ward, called to see a 67 year old man on the second day of admission for a chronic kidney disease stage 4 exacerbation. He was reviewed at handover this morning after commencing perindopril 4 mg for hypertension yesterday; his afternoon urea, electrolytes and creatinine result has been flagged for review.

On assessment he is asymptomatic apart from mild lethargy and denies chest pain, palpitations or focal weakness. His medications include perindopril 4 mg (new), amlodipine 5 mg, spironolactone 25 mg (six months), and metoprolol 25 mg twice daily.

His rhythm strip shows a broad regular tachycardia with peaked T waves in leads V2 to V4 and QRS 140 ms; there is no evidence of P waves. His most recent creatinine is 260 micromol/L (baseline 220).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 /min, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, chest clear, no oedema, no focal neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 7.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), sodium 138 mmol/L, creatinine 260 micromol/L (baseline 220), bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, glucose 6.8 mmol/L, ECG: broad QRS 140 ms with peaked T waves and absent P waves

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Administer 50 mL of 50% dextrose with 10 units of actrapid insulin intravenously
options.rationale: Insulin plus glucose is the correct SECOND step because it drives potassium into cells, but the immediate priority with. (Source: eTG: Renal)

options.text: Commence intravenous furosemide 40 mg and 1 L of 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Furosemide and volume can drop potassium slowly through renal excretion but do NOT protect the myocardium during acute E. (Source: eTG: Renal)

options.text: Cease perindopril and spironolactone and recheck potassium in one hour
options.rationale: Stopping the offending drugs is essential but does not treat the immediate arrhythmic risk. Do both, but calcium first. (Source: eTG: Renal)

options.text: Give calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL intravenously over 2 to 5 minutes
options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia with broad QRS, peaked T waves and absent P waves has ECG changes threatening ventricular arrhythmia. (Source: eTG: Renal; ANZCOR)

options.text: Give oral resonium 30 g and reassess electrolytes in six hours
options.rationale: Cation-exchange resins act slowly (hours) and do not protect the myocardium; they are adjuncts, not first-line for acute. (Source: eTG: Renal)

explanation.summary: Acute severe hyperkalaemia (potassium >6.5 or ECG changes) is a medical emergency because progressive changes go from peaked T waves to PR prolongation to QRS widening to sine-wave.
key_points: Peaked T waves progress to broad QRS to sine-wave to VF.
Calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV over 2-5 minutes stabilises the myocardium first.
Insulin plus glucose and salbutamol shift potassium into cells.
explanation.pearls: In hyperkalaemia with a broad QRS, give calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 2 to 5 minutes FIRST; insulin-glucose comes second.

subtopic_detail: PE evaluation with age-adjusted D-dimer
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing an 82 year old woman with one day of pleuritic right-sided chest pain and mild breathlessness. She was well until yesterday; there has been no immobilisation, no recent surgery, and no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism. Her only medications are amlodipine 5 mg and atorvastatin 20 mg.

She denies calf swelling, haemoptysis, syncope, and constitutional symptoms. Her observations are stable and there is no clinical deep vein thrombosis. Chest X-ray is unremarkable.

Her PE Wells score is 1.5 (based on 'PE is the most likely diagnosis' 3 points is not scored; 'no alternative diagnosis' scored 3 - wait re-review). Applying the two-tier Wells score she scores 3 (clinical signs of DVT 0, PE more likely than alternative diagnosis 3), placing her in the 'PE likely' group per the two-tier system.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, chest clear, no calf tenderness, no swelling, no haemoptysis
data_table.Investigations: Chest X-ray unremarkable, ECG sinus rhythm 88/min without S1Q3T3 or right heart strain, D-dimer 640 microg/L (units are FEUs; conventional cut-off 500 microg/L)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure and discharge because D-dimer only mildly exceeds 500 microg/L today and imaging is not required
options.rationale: Age-adjusted D-dimer for patients over 50 uses a cut-off of age x 10 microg/L (up to 82 years so 820 microg/L). (Source: eTG: Respiratory; NICE PE)

options.text: Repeat D-dimer at 24 hours using an age-adjusted cut-off before deciding on imaging or discharge home
options.rationale: Serial D-dimers do not have a defined role in acute PE diagnosis; the algorithm is Wells then either D-dimer for rule-ou. (Source: eTG: Respiratory)

options.text: Arrange ventilation-perfusion scan first because of her age and preferred low contrast exposure pathway
options.rationale: V/Q scan is preferred over CTPA when renal function is poor, contrast is contraindicated, or in pregnancy; her creatinin. (Source: eTG: Respiratory)

options.text: Start therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily and image in 24 hours to avoid immediate CT pathway
options.rationale: Empirical anticoagulation is reasonable when imaging is delayed beyond 4 hours in a stable, high-risk patient, but immed. (Source: eTG: Respiratory)

options.text: Perform CT pulmonary angiography now given the two-tier Wells score places her in the PE-likely group
options.rationale: In the 2-tier Wells rule, a score over 4 is 'PE likely' and mandates CT pulmonary angiography (or V/Q if renal function. (Source: eTG: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: The two-tier Wells score assigns patients to 'PE unlikely' (score 4 or less) or 'PE likely' (over 4).
key_points: Wells 2-tier: 4 or less is unlikely; over 4 is likely.
D-dimer rules out only in 'PE unlikely' - do not apply in likely group.
Age-adjusted D-dimer cut-off: age x 10 microg/L over 50 years (FEU units).
explanation.pearls: In 'PE likely' Wells patients, image directly with CTPA; D-dimer belongs to the 'PE unlikely' rule-out arm only.

subtopic_detail: Infective endocarditis empirical therapy by valve type
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58 year old man on the ward with fever for six days, malaise and a five kilogram weight loss over the last month. He had a mitral valve prosthesis inserted two years ago for endocarditis complicating rheumatic heart disease. He denies IV drug use, recent dental work, or urinary or respiratory symptoms.

On examination he has a new murmur, one Roth spot on fundoscopy, and one tender nodule on the pulp of his left index finger. Three sets of blood cultures have been drawn at least an hour apart from separate venepuncture sites in the last 12 hours; each has returned positive with gram-positive cocci in clusters, staphylococci pending speciation.

His transthoracic echocardiogram shows a 12 mm mobile echodensity attached to the mitral prosthetic ring; transoesophageal echocardiogram is scheduled for tomorrow.

options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin is empirical for streptococcal or enterococcal native-valve endocarditis, not staphyloc. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic; Australian endocarditis guidelines)

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis in intercurrent illness
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to see a 42 year old man with primary adrenal insufficiency (autoimmune Addison disease diagnosed 8 years ago) admitted 12 hours ago with community-acquired pneumonia. He is normally on hydrocortisone 20 mg on waking plus 10 mg at midday plus fludrocortisone 100 microgram in the morning. On admission he was told to double his hydrocortisone dose while unwell but has been vomiting since he arrived and has not kept anything down.

He was reviewed by the intern earlier and given intravenous ceftriaxone and 1 L of 0.9% sodium chloride. His observations show tachycardia and postural drop; the nurse escalates because he has become confused and is complaining of severe abdominal pain and worsening lethargy.

On examination he is agitated and clammy. Abdominal examination is soft with no peritonism.

options.rationale: Adrenal crisis in an established Addison patient with intercurrent sepsis, vomiting, hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperka. (Source: eTG: Endocrinology; Endocrine Society)

options.text: Give intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg because it will not interfere with the cortisol assay result immediately

options.text: Give oral hydrocortisone 40 mg plus antiemetic ondansetron 4 mg intravenously in the same treatment window
options.rationale: Oral therapy is not reliable in a vomiting hypotensive patient; parenteral hydrocortisone is essential. (Source: eTG: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give a 500 mL 5% dextrose bolus and start a fludrocortisone infusion to correct volume and mineralocorticoid
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is oral and slow-acting; it is not first-line in acute crisis when high-dose hydrocortisone covers miner. (Source: eTG: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is precipitated by inability to increase steroid replacement in intercurrent illness (infection, surgery, trauma) or by missed doses in an established primary or sec.
key_points: Adrenal crisis: hypotension, vomiting, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia in known adrenal.
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately then 200 mg per 24 hours; do not wait for cortisol result.
0.9% sodium chloride resuscitation and glucose replacement.

subtopic_detail: Diabetic foot osteomyelitis diagnostic pathway and antibiotic duration
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 62 year old man with type 2 diabetes for 20 years and peripheral neuropathy. He presents with a plantar ulcer over the fifth metatarsal head that has been present for eight weeks. He has attended community wound care but the ulcer has not healed. He has never had osteomyelitis.

On examination the ulcer is 2 cm across with granulating base; a sterile probe passes freely to bone at the base of the ulcer. He is systemically well with normal observations. There is no cellulitis and no fluctuance.

Plain radiograph shows subtle cortical erosion under the fifth metatarsal head; ESR is 96 mm/h and CRP 42 mg/L. HbA1c is 79 mmol/mol.

data_table.Examination: 2 cm plantar ulcer over fifth metatarsal head with clean granulating base, probe-to-bone positive, no cellulitis, no fluctuance, reduced monofilament sensation to ankle
data_table.Investigations: ESR 96 mm/h (<15), CRP 42 mg/L (<5), HbA1c 79 mmol/mol, creatinine 92 micromol/L, white cell count 8.4 x10^9/L, foot X-ray: subtle cortical erosion at fifth metatarsal head

options.text: Request nuclear medicine bone scan and treat with amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily while awaiting results
options.rationale: MRI is more specific than bone scan in the diabetic foot, and empirical narrow-spectrum oral therapy without cultures ri. (Source: IWGDF diabetic foot)

subtopic_detail: Massive haemoptysis - lateral positioning and bronchial arteriography
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department when a 54 year old man with long-standing bronchiectasis is brought in by ambulance. He has coughed up around 350 mL of fresh red blood over the last 40 minutes in three episodes at home. His observations on arrival: pulse 128, BP 96/60, SpO2 92% on 10 L via non-rebreather. Chest X-ray shows dense right upper zone consolidation.

You know from previous imaging that his major cavity is right upper lobe, and multiple prior CT reports have suggested his bleeding is right-sided.

He has continued to spit bright red blood into the emesis bag during the initial assessment; the anaesthetic and interventional radiology teams have been paged.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 /min, SpO2 92% on 10 L non-rebreather, temperature 37.2 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, coughing bright red blood, chest crackles bilaterally worse right upper zone, fresh blood on lips, no obvious epistaxis
data_table.Investigations: Bedside haemoglobin 96 g/L (baseline 128), INR 1.1, platelets 168 x10^9/L, chest X-ray: dense right upper zone opacity with air bronchograms

lead_in: What is the single best immediate management step (before definitive bronchial artery embolisation)?

options.text: Perform emergency CT pulmonary angiogram before any positioning change or airway intervention or transfer
options.rationale: CT is often part of the workup but positioning and haemostasis come first; imaging in a critically bleeding, unstable pa. (Source: TSANZ)

options.text: Position supine with head-up tilt, intubate, and start intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes now
options.rationale: Supine positioning risks flooding the good lung with blood. Bleeding-side down protects the unaffected lung. (Source: TSANZ)

options.text: Start non-invasive ventilation and give nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 solution as first-line control
options.rationale: NIV in massive haemoptysis risks aspiration; the priority is protection of the unaffected lung with positioning and cons. (Source: TSANZ)

options.text: Right lateral decubitus positioning (bleeding-side down), activate massive transfusion, expedite embolisation
options.rationale: In massive haemoptysis the priority is to prevent aspiration to the unaffected lung: lie the patient bleeding-side down. (Source: eTG: Respiratory; TSANZ)

options.text: Refer directly to thoracic surgery for emergency lobectomy without prior imaging or bronchial artery embolisation
options.rationale: Bronchial artery embolisation is first-line for non-traumatic massive haemoptysis and is less morbid than emergency lobe. (Source: TSANZ)

explanation.summary: Massive haemoptysis (typically >100 mL/hour or >600 mL/24 hours) is life-threatening because a small amount of blood floods alveoli and causes asphyxia.
key_points: Massive haemoptysis kills by asphyxia not exsanguination; protect the unaffected lung first.
Bleeding-side-down positioning or selective mainstem intubation.
Bronchial artery embolisation is definitive first-line (90% of bleeding is BA source).
explanation.pearls: In right-sided massive haemoptysis lie the patient right-side down to protect the left lung, then expedite bronchial artery embolisation; do NOT sit them uprigh.

subtopic_detail: Ischaemic stroke thrombolysis contraindications with recent surgery
stem:
You are the stroke registrar in a comprehensive stroke centre reviewing a 68 year old woman brought in by ambulance with left facial droop and right arm weakness noted by her husband on waking 90 minutes ago. She was last known well when she went to bed at 22:00 the previous night. Non-contrast CT brain excludes haemorrhage and shows a subtle hyperdense right middle cerebral artery sign; CT angiogram confirms right M1 occlusion; CT perfusion shows a small ischaemic core with a large penumbra.

Her history includes an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy nine days ago. She is otherwise on aspirin 100 mg only. There is no history of intracerebral haemorrhage, no recent significant head trauma, and no active bleeding.

Her blood pressure is 172/94, glucose 6.8 mmol/L, INR 1.0, and platelets 260 x10^9/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 172/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: NIHSS 12: left facial droop, right arm 2/5, right leg 4/5, dysarthria, right hemianopia; laparoscopic port sites healing
data_table.Investigations: Non-contrast CT: hyperdense right MCA sign, no haemorrhage. CT angiogram: right M1 occlusion. CT perfusion: core 12 mL, penumbra 88 mL, mismatch ratio 8. INR 1.0, platelets 260, glucose 6.8

lead_in: What is the single best next step in reperfusion management?

options.text: Give intravenous tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg then transfer immediately for endovascular thrombectomy on M1 lesion
options.rationale: Major surgery within 14 days is a relative contraindication to IV thrombolysis because of bleeding risk at the surgical. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia guidelines)

options.text: Await MRI diffusion-weighted imaging before deciding on any reperfusion strategy including thrombectomy today
options.rationale: MRI DWI-FLAIR mismatch is used in wake-up strokes when CT perfusion is not available; here CT perfusion already shows fa. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia guidelines)

options.text: Manage with intravenous aspirin 300 mg and admission to the stroke unit without any reperfusion intervention
options.rationale: Aspirin alone in a large-vessel occlusion with substantial penumbra fails to restore flow and misses the reperfusion win. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia guidelines)

options.text: Give reduced-dose alteplase 0.6 mg/kg and defer endovascular thrombectomy for 24 hours awaiting stability
options.rationale: Reduced-dose alteplase is not a standard Australian practice; recent surgery makes thrombolysis unsafe and delaying thro. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia guidelines)

options.text: Proceed directly to endovascular thrombectomy without intravenous thrombolysis given the recent 9-day surgery
options.rationale: Ischaemic stroke with large vessel occlusion and favourable core-penumbra mismatch is a thrombectomy indication regardle. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia guidelines; DIRECT-MT)

explanation.summary: Modern ischaemic stroke reperfusion has two strands: intravenous thrombolysis (tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg or alteplase) within 4.5 hours from onset or within an extended wake-up windo.
key_points: Large-vessel occlusion with favourable imaging is a thrombectomy indication regardless of thrombolys.
Thrombolysis is contraindicated with major surgery within 14 days.
Direct-to-thrombectomy is Australian standard when thrombolysis carries additional risk.
explanation.pearls: Recent major surgery within 14 days makes IV thrombolysis unsafe, but does NOT contraindicate endovascular thrombectomy; go direct to clot retrieval.
